questions.q: Why is a field-level ownership matrix necessary even after Lesson 1's domain-level system-of-record split is in place?
options: Domain-level ownership ('the ERP owns pricing') doesn't specify who owns each individual shared field on a shared object like Account, leaving that as an implicit, unreviewed assumption
Field-level matrices are required by Salesforce's terms of service
Field-level ownership replaces the need for External IDs
Domain-level ownership only applies to custom objects, not standard objects
questions.explain: A shared object can have many fields with different natural owners; the domain-level split doesn't resolve field-by-field ownership on its own, which is exactly the gap the field-level matrix closes.

questions.q: What problem does a canonical data model solve in a CRM+ERP integration?
options: It eliminates the need for any field mapping entirely
It automatically resolves every conflict without a resolution rule
It gives the integration layer one shared, system-neutral definition of a concept, so translation logic isn't scattered ad hoc across every sync job that touches that field
It is only relevant when more than ten systems are integrated
questions.explain: Without a canonical model, each sync job re-implements its own translation between the two systems' different shapes for the same concept, which gets worse as more systems join the integration.

questions.q: When is 'system-of-record wins' the appropriate conflict-resolution rule, per this lesson?
options: For any field, regardless of ownership
For a field that already has a clearly owned system -- the owning system's value always wins, and the other system's copy should be read-only
Only for fields with no assigned owner
Only when both systems' clocks are perfectly synchronized
questions.explain: Once a field has an assigned owner, system-of-record-wins is the natural rule -- the non-owning system's copy is a reflection that shouldn't have been independently editable in the first place.

questions.q: What assumption does last-write-wins by timestamp depend on in order to work safely?
options: That the field in question has no assigned owner at all
That the two systems never update the field within the same calendar day
That the field is never displayed on a Salesforce page layout
That both systems' clocks are reliably synchronized and the sync records a trustworthy timestamp
questions.explain: Timestamp-based conflict resolution is only valid if the timestamps being compared are actually trustworthy and the clocks that produced them are synchronized -- an assumption worth explicitly testing.

questions.q: What is 'silent last-write-wins,' and why is it called out as a failure mode rather than a legitimate strategy?
options: It's a documented Salesforce feature that should be enabled by default
It's a setting that silences error notifications for failed syncs
It's an outcome where nobody explicitly chose a conflict rule, and the sync job's accidental execution order ends up deciding the result -- an unreviewed side effect, not a deliberate policy
It only occurs when External ID fields are misconfigured
questions.explain: The distinction is intent: a deliberately chosen last-write-wins rule with reliable timestamps is a real policy, while silent last-write-wins is an unreviewed accident of execution order that happens to look fine until two near-simultaneous updates expose it.
